[2] The claimants fear arrest by the Public Security Bureau (PSB) because the principal claimant and the female claimant both opposed the expropriation of their land by the government. In April 1996, the principal claimant signed a contract to lease a fish pond for ten years. In April 2006, the principal claimant renewed the contract for twenty years; at this time, he also expanded his fish pond. On January 12, 2012, the principal claimant received a notice from the district government that they wanted to take away his fish pond because they needed it as part of the land to build a logistics distribution centre. He was informed that he had to vacate the land by the end of March, 2012. The principal claimant's fish pond was among one of twenty seven businesses affected by this notice by the government.

[3] The business owners occupying the land were offered only small amount of cash as compensation. The claimants, along with other business owners affected by the proposal, approached the district authorities on several occasions; however, their efforts produced no positive results. Thereafter, the business owners decided to go to higher levels of the government. They approached the municipal government as well as the provincial government; they were told that they must go back to the district government as the district government was the only authority that could deal with the matter.

[4] On February 21, 2012, the business owners went to the district government office and put up a demonstration. Since no one from the district government responded, they returned the next day to continue their demonstration. On this second day of demonstration, the police came to the scene and confronted the demonstrators. There were clashes between the police and the demonstrators. Several of the demonstrators were detained by the police. The principal claimant and the female claimant managed to escape the scene, and thereafter went into hiding; their son stayed at their home with his grandparents.

[5] While the principal claimant and the female claimant were in hiding, the principal claimant's parents informed them that the PSB had gone to their home to arrest the principal claimant and the female claimant. The PSB also questioned the son about his parents' whereabouts; he was threatened that if he did not cooperate, he would face consequences. Since the PSB continued to harass the family to disclose the whereabouts of the principal claimant and the female claimant, the son went into hiding in late February, 2012; he joined his parents who were already in hiding. While in hiding, the claimants found a smuggler who made all the arrangements for them to flee China.

[6] On XXXX XXXX, 2012, the claimants arrived in the United States of America (U.S.). On XXXX XXXX, 2012, the claimants crossed the U.S.-Canada border into Vancouver illegally, and arrived in Canada. They filed their claims for refugee protection at an inland office of the Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC).
DETERMINATION

[7] The panel determines that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

The principal claimant testified that six of the eight demonstrators arrested have been released; two persons still continued to be detained. The principal claimant did not know why different people got different sentences. Based on the totality of the evidence in this case, the panel finds that the PSB, on a balance of probabilities, arrested demonstrators who were involved in clashes with the PSB. The principal claimant testified that he was not among those in clashes with the PSB. The claimants learned from the principal claimant's parents that the PSB had gone to their home on February 23, 2012, to arrest them. Based on the evidence in this case, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, these claimants were not pursued by the PSB on February 23, 2012 as alleged.
Arrests of three elected representatives/demonstrators during clashes with the PSB

[27] The principal claimant testified that the PSB would arrest him upon return to China because he is one of the six elected representatives. He added that three of the six elected representatives were arrested and have still not been released. He testified that he learnt from his father that two of the six elected representatives have fled to South America. The panel pointed it to the principal claimant that his father had not mentioned in his letter10 that two of the six elected representatives have fled China and went to South America; he replied that he had learnt about this in his conversations with his father over the telephone. The panel notes that the information about two of the elected representatives having fled to South America is also not included in the claimants' addendum to the narrative,11 dated September 15, 2017. The panel finds this omission from the claimants' documentary evidence to be significant. This information goes to the heart of these claims. The panel draws negative inference from this omission from the claimants' own personal documentary evidence.
PSB's continued visits from 2012 onwards; no summons and/or arrest warrants issued

[28] The claimants alleged that the PSB has continued to visit their home since 2012. The claimants' evidence, however, shows that the frequency of home visits decreased after it was disclosed to the PSB that the claimants have fled China and gone abroad. It is added though that the PSB still continued to visit their home at the end of each October and around the Chinese New Year.12 The claimants were asked if they have any documents to corroborate that the PSB has continued to pursue to locate these claimants. The claimants testified that the PSB has not left any documentation at their house. In light of the alleged risk of persecution at the hands of the PSB, the panel finds it not credible, on a balance of probabilities, that the PSB would be visiting these claimants' home on numerous occasions, over a span of several years, yet leave no Summons or Arrest Warrant with their family. The panel finds this finding further detracts from the claimants' credibility in that the PSB has continued to locate these claimants to arrest them as alleged.

[29] The claimants travelled from Guangzhou to Hong Kong by train, and then took a flight from Hong Kong to San Francisco. The claimants did not request asylum in the U.S.; instead they crossed the U.S.-Canada border illegally, and then filed their claims for refugee protection at an inland office of the IRCC. [30] Failure to seek the protection of another country which is also a signatory to the Convention may be a significant factor to consider but is not in itself determinative. Case law states that a negative inference can be drawn from a claimant's failure to claim in a safe third country, but it also clearly states that this failure cannot be determinative.13 In this respect, the Court has also frequently held that a short stay in a safe third country en route to Canada is not necessarily considered a sufficiently material enough sojourn to create an expectation that the claimant would claim refugee status during that stay.14 Where a claimant had always planned to come to Canada, and merely was in transit during a stopover in a third country, the Court has held that such a situation does not undermine the subjective fear of persecution.15

[31] The panel can accept that the claimants might have hired a smuggler to assist them with their plans to come to Canada. The panel, however, does not, on a balance of probabilities, find it credible that the claimants hired the smuggler for the alleged purpose of fleeing China, i.e., because they were afraid to be arrested by the PSB as alleged and thus were in hiding all along before they left China. The panel finds these claimants, on a balance of probabilities, made plans to come to Canada to reside and hired a smuggler to help them execute their plans. [37] An undated article on the website of the Ministry of Public Security, entitled: "Deepening the Implementation of the 'Golden Shield' Project" states that:
... all police units nationwide have access to eight public security databases, including the "National Basic Population Information Database". Also accessible through the databases is information on household registration [hukou], border exit and entry, road traffic, and criminal investigations.21 [footnote omitted]

[38] In addition, the representative of the Laogai Research Foundation provided the following information:
The Golden Shield incorporates extensive tracking and control mechanisms such as real-name online registration requirements, GPS monitoring, and facial recognition surveillance technology in a multi-pronged approach to identify potentially disruptive individuals. Policenet, a component of the Golden Shield, stores a wealth of information on Chinese citizens and connects the various agencies and levels of command within the public security apparatus. This integrated system enables Chinese public security forces to effectively target and neutralize political dissidents.22

[39] The panel finds that, in light of the claimants' allegations that the PSB were pursuing them and wanted to arrest them, it is reasonable to expect that the local authorities would have entered their information into the database to further the PSB's efforts to apprehend these claimants.

[40] The panel has considered that the claimants used a smuggler to exit China. However, the panel finds that the objective evidence concerning the Golden Shield and other border controls in place at exit points, including railway stations and airports, in China is compelling and convincing. While it might be possible for a smuggler to bypass some of the security controls, based on the evidence in the record, the panel finds it less likely than more, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants could have bypassed all of the security controls in place if they were being actively pursued by the PSB as alleged.

[41] The panel is entitled to make reasonable findings based on implausibilities, common sense and rationality, and it may reject evidence if it is not consistent with the probabilities affecting the case as a whole.23 Where the panel finds a lack of credibility based on inferences concerning the plausibility of evidence, there must be a basis in the evidence to support such inferences.24 In this case, the panel finds there is an evidentiary foundation for the negative credibility findings.

REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] XXXX XXXX (the principal claimant), his wife XXXX XXXX (the female claimant), and their son, XXXX XXXX (the son), are citizens of China. They are claiming refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act ("IRPA").1
BACKGROUND/ALLEGATIONS

[2] The claimants fear arrest by the Public Security Bureau (PSB) because the principal claimant and the female claimant both opposed the expropriation of their land by the government. In April 1996, the principal claimant signed a contract to lease a fish pond for ten years. In April 2006, the principal claimant renewed the contract for twenty years; at this time, he also expanded his fish pond. On January 12, 2012, the principal claimant received a notice from the district government that they wanted to take away his fish pond because they needed it as part of the land to build a logistics distribution centre. He was informed that he had to vacate the land by the end of March, 2012. The principal claimant's fish pond was among one of twenty seven businesses affected by this notice by the government.

[3] The business owners occupying the land were offered only small amount of cash as compensation. The claimants, along with other business owners affected by the proposal, approached the district authorities on several occasions; however, their efforts produced no positive results. Thereafter, the business owners decided to go to higher levels of the government. They approached the municipal government as well as the provincial government; they were told that they must go back to the district government as the district government was the only authority that could deal with the matter.

[4] On February 21, 2012, the business owners went to the district government office and put up a demonstration. Since no one from the district government responded, they returned the next day to continue their demonstration. On this second day of demonstration, the police came to the scene and confronted the demonstrators. There were clashes between the police and the demonstrators. Several of the demonstrators were detained by the police. The principal claimant and the female claimant managed to escape the scene, and thereafter went into hiding; their son stayed at their home with his grandparents.

[5] While the principal claimant and the female claimant were in hiding, the principal claimant's parents informed them that the PSB had gone to their home to arrest the principal claimant and the female claimant. The PSB also questioned the son about his parents' whereabouts; he was threatened that if he did not cooperate, he would face consequences. Since the PSB continued to harass the family to disclose the whereabouts of the principal claimant and the female claimant, the son went into hiding in late February, 2012; he joined his parents who were already in hiding. While in hiding, the claimants found a smuggler who made all the arrangements for them to flee China.

[6] On XXXX XXXX, 2012, the claimants arrived in the United States of America (U.S.). On XXXX XXXX, 2012, the claimants crossed the U.S.-Canada border into Vancouver illegally, and arrived in Canada. They filed their claims for refugee protection at an inland office of the Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC).
DETERMINATION

[7] The panel determines that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.
IDENTITY

[8] Based on certified true copies of the claimants' Chinese passports2 and other documents3 in evidence, the panel accepts that the claimants are citizens of China.
DETERMINATIVE ISSUES

[9] The determinative issue in these claims are credibility, and whether what they fear upon return is prosecution and not persecution.
COUNSEL'S ORAL APPLICATION FOR THE MEMBER TO RECUSE HERSELF

[10] The claimants held that the PSB has continued to visit their home in China even after the principal claimant's father told the PSB that the claimants have left China and gone abroad. The panel expressed credibility concerns around the claimants' evidence that the PSB had visited the claimants' home on numerous occasions over the years, especially in that the PSB continued to visit their home in China even after the principal claimant's father told the PSB that the claimants have left China and gone abroad. The claimants submitted no documents from the authorities showing that they have been pursuing to locate these claimants. Within this context, the panel stated that it is "odd" and added that it "does not make sense" that the PSB would not leave any documentation whatsoever during any of their numerous alleged visits to the claimants' home spanning several years, i.e., from 2012 to 2017.
[11] In response to the panel's stating the above-mentioned concerns, the claimants' counsel made an oral application for the panel member to recuse herself due to an apprehension of bias.

[12] The panel addressed counsel's motion at the hearing. At the hearing, the panel member provided reasons for her decision not to recuse herself. The panel considered whether any of her comments made at the hearing could constitute a valid ground for a reasonable apprehension of bias, and applied the test for bias.
[13] The panel believes reasons provided at the hearing were sufficient. The panel, however, adds the following herein.

[14] The common-law principles of natural justice are recognized in section 162(2) of the IRPA:
Each Division shall deal with all proceedings before it as informally and quickly as the circumstances and the considerations of fairness and natural justice permit.

[15] The principles of natural justice include the common-law rule against bias. That rule disqualifies a decision-maker from determining any case in which there is actual bias or an appearance of bias, also described as a reasonable apprehension of bias.

[16] The test for a "reasonable apprehension of bias" was formulated by the Supreme Court of Canada in Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board:4
What would an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically - and having thought the matter through - conclude? Would he think that it is more likely than not that [the decision-maker], whether consciously or unconsciously, would not decide fairly.
[17] That Court also held that such a test should not be related to the "very sensitive or scrupulous conscience."5

[18] Clear evidence is required to support an allegation of bias. The Federal Court reiterated in Ali that:
... the Court of Appeal in Arthur v. Canada (Attorney General), has emphasized that an allegation of bias cannot be done lightly. It cannot rest on mere suspicion, pure conjecture or mere impressions of an applicant. It must be supported by material evidence.6 [footnotes omitted]

[19] The panel finds that an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically, and having thought it through, could not reasonably conclude in this case that the panel member, consciously or unconsciously, would not decide these claims fairly.

[20] The panel is required to adhere to the provisions of the Code of Conduct and the Conflict of Interest Act, and to make decisions fairly based on the evidence presented. There is no evidence that this panel would not do so. When this member was employed at the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada, the member swore to perform her duties as a member in compliance with these instruments. It is the duty of RPD members under the Code of Conduct for Members of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada, to decide every case on its merits and to not be influenced by any extraneous factors.

[21] The panel is of the view that the reasonable apprehension of bias raised by counsel has no basis in fact, is speculative and unsupported by any evidence whatsoever. The panel holds that, despite Counsel's oral application for the panel member to recuse herself, and allegations in order to get a de novo hearing, the claimants in the present case received a fair hearing.
ANALYSIS

[22] In making the determination in this case, the panel considered the totality of the evidence submitted/adduced, including the claimants' testimonies and their counsel's submissions.
Credibility

[23] When a claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are indeed true unless there is valid reason to doubt their veracity.7 The panel is aware that the real test of the truth of a story of a witness is that it be in harmony with the preponderance of probabilities, which a practical and informed person would readily recognize as reasonable in that place and in those conditions.8 Furthermore, the panel cannot be satisfied that, "the evidence is credible or trustworthy, unless satisfied that it is probably so, not just possibly so".9 The determination, as to whether a claimant's evidence is credible, is made on a balance of probabilities.

[24] In assessing credibility, the panel is cognizant of the many difficulties faced by the refugee claimant in establishing a claim, including cultural factors, the milieu of the hearing room, and the stress inherent in responding to oral questions through an interpreter.

[25] These claimants' problems started on or around February 22, 2012. The same day the principal claimant and the female claimant went into hiding. Their son stayed with the principal claimant's parents. The principal claimant and the female claimant alleged that the PSB visited their home and asked the principal claimant's parents and their son about their whereabouts. Approximately a week later, their son left the house and joined his parents in hiding. The claimants arranged for a smuggler to help them acquire U.S. visas and facilitate their exit from China. The claimants remained in hiding until they fled China.
Arrests of eight demonstrators during clashes with the PSB

[26] The claimants' evidence is that on the second day of demonstrations, on February 22, 2012, there were clashes between the PSB and the demonstrators; as a result, the PSB arrested eleven demonstrators, including three elected representatives. The principal claimant testified that six of the eight demonstrators arrested have been released; two persons still continued to be detained. The principal claimant did not know why different people got different sentences. Based on the totality of the evidence in this case, the panel finds that the PSB, on a balance of probabilities, arrested demonstrators who were involved in clashes with the PSB. The principal claimant testified that he was not among those in clashes with the PSB. The claimants learned from the principal claimant's parents that the PSB had gone to their home on February 23, 2012, to arrest them. Based on the evidence in this case, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, these claimants were not pursued by the PSB on February 23, 2012 as alleged.
Arrests of three elected representatives/demonstrators during clashes with the PSB

[27] The principal claimant testified that the PSB would arrest him upon return to China because he is one of the six elected representatives. He added that three of the six elected representatives were arrested and have still not been released. He testified that he learnt from his father that two of the six elected representatives have fled to South America. The panel pointed it to the principal claimant that his father had not mentioned in his letter10 that two of the six elected representatives have fled China and went to South America; he replied that he had learnt about this in his conversations with his father over the telephone. The panel notes that the information about two of the elected representatives having fled to South America is also not included in the claimants' addendum to the narrative,11 dated September 15, 2017. The panel finds this omission from the claimants' documentary evidence to be significant. This information goes to the heart of these claims. The panel draws negative inference from this omission from the claimants' own personal documentary evidence.
PSB's continued visits from 2012 onwards; no summons and/or arrest warrants issued

[28] The claimants alleged that the PSB has continued to visit their home since 2012. The claimants' evidence, however, shows that the frequency of home visits decreased after it was disclosed to the PSB that the claimants have fled China and gone abroad. It is added though that the PSB still continued to visit their home at the end of each October and around the Chinese New Year.12 The claimants were asked if they have any documents to corroborate that the PSB has continued to pursue to locate these claimants. The claimants testified that the PSB has not left any documentation at their house. In light of the alleged risk of persecution at the hands of the PSB, the panel finds it not credible, on a balance of probabilities, that the PSB would be visiting these claimants' home on numerous occasions, over a span of several years, yet leave no Summons or Arrest Warrant with their family. The panel finds this finding further detracts from the claimants' credibility in that the PSB has continued to locate these claimants to arrest them as alleged.
Failure to seek asylum in the U.S.

[29] The claimants travelled from Guangzhou to Hong Kong by train, and then took a flight from Hong Kong to San Francisco. The claimants did not request asylum in the U.S.; instead they crossed the U.S.-Canada border illegally, and then filed their claims for refugee protection at an inland office of the IRCC. The claimants' explanation for their failure to seek asylum in the U.S. was that the smuggler had suggested that Canada would be a better place for them to claim asylum.

[30] Failure to seek the protection of another country which is also a signatory to the Convention may be a significant factor to consider but is not in itself determinative. Case law states that a negative inference can be drawn from a claimant's failure to claim in a safe third country, but it also clearly states that this failure cannot be determinative.13 In this respect, the Court has also frequently held that a short stay in a safe third country en route to Canada is not necessarily considered a sufficiently material enough sojourn to create an expectation that the claimant would claim refugee status during that stay.14 Where a claimant had always planned to come to Canada, and merely was in transit during a stopover in a third country, the Court has held that such a situation does not undermine the subjective fear of persecution.15

[31] The panel can accept that the claimants might have hired a smuggler to assist them with their plans to come to Canada. The panel, however, does not, on a balance of probabilities, find it credible that the claimants hired the smuggler for the alleged purpose of fleeing China, i.e., because they were afraid to be arrested by the PSB as alleged and thus were in hiding all along before they left China. The panel finds these claimants, on a balance of probabilities, made plans to come to Canada to reside and hired a smuggler to help them execute their plans. This finding detracts from their credibility.

[32] The panel finds that the claimants' failure to claim asylum in the U.S. and entering Canada illegally is indicative of a lack of subjective fear.
Claimants' ability to leave China while being pursued by the PSB

[33] The panel finds it not credible that the claimants could go through China's strict exit controls if they were truly wanted for arrest by the PSB. The panel is aware that the claimants alleged to have hired a smuggler to assist them with their international travel. In consideration of the totality of the evidence, however, the panel finds the claimants not credible in that they are wanted by the PSB for arrest as alleged. In this context, in consideration of the totality of the documentary evidence in this case, the panel is not persuaded by the claimants' argument that the smuggler made all the arrangements, including their evasion of security checks upon existing China.

[34] The claimants travelled from mainland China to Hong Kong, and then from Hong Kong to San Francisco. The national documentation sources report that the Chinese authorities consider travel from mainland China to Hong Kong as international travel; and that they apply the same level of security and immigration screening for exits from mainland China for travel to Hong Kong as they do for all international travel departing mainland China.16

[35] The panel also finds that the documentary evidence reveals that the Chinese government has a national computer network known as the Golden Shield Project,17 and the PSB has access to a national policing database, which includes information about criminal fugitives and information on passports and exit and entry. The Golden Shield incorporated extensive tracking and control mechanisms including facial recognition surveillance technology.

[36] The panel also notes that the documentation states that security officials have access to the Public Security Bureau of China's online database of citizens who have been convicted of crimes or are wanted by the authorities (also known as Policenet or the Golden Shield).18
(...) Information Sharing by Public Security Officials
In 10 February 2014 correspondence with the Research Directorate, the Executive Director of the Dui Hua Foundation affirmed that airport security officials have access to the Public Security Bureau of China's online database of citizens who have been convicted of crimes or are wanted by the authorities [also known as Policenet or the Golden Shield]. Similarly, the representative of the Laogai Research Foundation stated that reports on "experiences of activists who have been detained while trying to board an international flight provide clear evidence that airport officials are connected to Policenet".
A colleague of Cao Shunli, who was also prevented from travelling to Geneva for the human rights training in September 2013, later publicized her own experience at the airport in Guangdong. According to the Laogai research Foundation, the colleague indicates that when her passport was swiped by airport authorities, scanning equipment immediately made noises alerting airport officials that she was wanted by police. She was subsequently detained in the Guangdong Baiyun Airport and told that Shanghai police would not let her leave. She was then transported from Guangdong to Shanghai for detention and questioning. This woman's experience provides concrete evidence of airport officials coordinating with police departments in tracking and detaining a political dissident.19 [footnotes omitted]
Security and Exit Control Procedures
The representative of the Laogai Research Foundation wrote that the Chinese government checks the passports of citizens attempting to leave the country in order to ensure that they are suitable for foreign travel. Customs officials stamp the passports of citizens approved for foreign travel. Public security officials often confiscate passports held by individuals deemed unsuitable for foreign travel.20 [footnotes omitted]

[37] An undated article on the website of the Ministry of Public Security, entitled: "Deepening the Implementation of the 'Golden Shield' Project" states that:
... all police units nationwide have access to eight public security databases, including the "National Basic Population Information Database". Also accessible through the databases is information on household registration [hukou], border exit and entry, road traffic, and criminal investigations.21 [footnote omitted]

[38] In addition, the representative of the Laogai Research Foundation provided the following information:
The Golden Shield incorporates extensive tracking and control mechanisms such as real-name online registration requirements, GPS monitoring, and facial recognition surveillance technology in a multi-pronged approach to identify potentially disruptive individuals. Policenet, a component of the Golden Shield, stores a wealth of information on Chinese citizens and connects the various agencies and levels of command within the public security apparatus. This integrated system enables Chinese public security forces to effectively target and neutralize political dissidents.22

[39] The panel finds that, in light of the claimants' allegations that the PSB were pursuing them and wanted to arrest them, it is reasonable to expect that the local authorities would have entered their information into the database to further the PSB's efforts to apprehend these claimants.

[40] The panel has considered that the claimants used a smuggler to exit China. However, the panel finds that the objective evidence concerning the Golden Shield and other border controls in place at exit points, including railway stations and airports, in China is compelling and convincing. While it might be possible for a smuggler to bypass some of the security controls, based on the evidence in the record, the panel finds it less likely than more, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants could have bypassed all of the security controls in place if they were being actively pursued by the PSB as alleged.

[41] The panel is entitled to make reasonable findings based on implausibilities, common sense and rationality, and it may reject evidence if it is not consistent with the probabilities affecting the case as a whole.23 Where the panel finds a lack of credibility based on inferences concerning the plausibility of evidence, there must be a basis in the evidence to support such inferences.24 In this case, the panel finds there is an evidentiary foundation for the negative credibility findings.

[42] The panel does not find it credible that the claimants were able to leave Mainland China and travel to Hong Kong, and then leave Hong Kong for international travel on their own passports after coming to the attention of the PSB as alleged. Therefore, the panel draws a negative inference as it relates to the credibility of the claimants' allegations that they were being pursued by the PSB as alleged.

[43] Based on the foregoing credibility findings, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, the claimants' allegations that they would face persecution due to their participation in the protest arising from the expropriation of their property to be not credible. The panel finds that the claimants have not provided sufficient credible and trustworthy probative evidence establishing that they are being pursued by the PSB for the purpose of arresting them.
Pursuit by the PSB for persons who participated in anti-government demonstrations

[44] Even if the panel were to believe that the PSB is looking for these claimants due to their participation in anti-government demonstration, the panel finds there is insufficient reliable and satisfactory probative evidence to find that these claimants are subject to persecution by the PSB or any other state authority in China for their alleged participation in anti-government demonstration.

[45] The documentary evidence reports:
'Chinese law criminalizes unauthorized demonstrations and those gathering to "disturb public order." Unauthorized assemblies are met with brutal force, arrests, detentions, and criminal penalties of up to five years in prison. In...China...no children, young adults, or foreigners are allowed to protest...25

[46] Despite, it is also reported that "[c]itizens continue to gather publicly to protest evictions, relocations and compensation in locations throughout the country, often resulting in conflict with authorities or other charges."26 Further, it is noted that "[a]uthorities use administrative detention to intimidate political activists and prevent public demonstrations."27

[47] In the circumstances of this case, the panel finds that any interest the PSB may have in these claimants, which the panel does not believe that they do, would be to prosecute them for breaking laws by participating in anti-government demonstration.
[48] Based on the foregoing analysis, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, these claimants are not being sought for arrest by the authorities in China as alleged.)

[49] Based on the totality of the evidence submitted/adduced in this case, the panel finds that the claimants have not satisfied their burden of establishing a serious possibility that they would be persecuted, or, that they would, on a balance of probabilities, be personally subjected to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture upon return to China today.
CONCLUSION
[50] Pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the IRPA, the panel finds that the claimants are neither Convention refugees, nor persons in need of protection.

[51] The claims are rejected.
